learn.title: Green Hydrogen Steel Production
learn.intro: Green steel uses hydrogen instead of coal in blast furnaces, cutting 75% of steelmaking emissions. This innovation is critical for decarbonizing heavy industry, a sector responsible for 7% of global CO2 emissions.
learn.c1_text: In traditional steelmaking, coal reacts with iron ore at 2,000°C to extract iron. Hydrogen acts as a cleaner 'reducing agent,' binding with oxygen to form water vapor instead of CO2. One ton of green steel avoids 1.8 tons of CO2 emissions compared to conventional methods.
learn.c2_text: The chemical reaction H2 + CO → H2O + C replaces carbon monoxide with water vapor. This shift reduces furnace emissions by 90% and aligns with the IEA's roadmap for net-zero steel by 2050.
learn.c3_text: India’s steel sector consumes 120 MT of coal annually. Projects like POSCO’s green steel plant in Gujarat aim to produce 5 MT/year using hydrogen, supported by a ₹10,000-crore government subsidy for clean tech.
learn.stat1: India’s steel sector emits 300 MT CO2/year (2023).
learn.stat2: Global green steel capacity could reach 100 MT/year by 2030.
learn.stat3: Hydrogen-based steel reduces energy use by 40% compared to coal.
learn.stat4: India plans 10 GW of renewable energy to power green steel plants by 2030.

learn.title: Demand Response Power Balancing
learn.intro: Large energy users like factories adjust consumption during peak grid stress, reducing strain and avoiding blackouts. This flexibility is key to integrating renewables and maintaining grid stability.
learn.c1_text: When solar/wind output drops, demand response programs signal factories to pause non-essential processes. For example, a textile plant might delay dyeing machines, saving 500 kWh during a grid crisis.
learn.c2_text: Grid operators use software to communicate with smart meters. When frequency dips below 49 Hz, signals trigger automated load shedding. This prevents cascading failures and integrates renewables’ variability.
learn.c3_text: India’s 2023 National Electricity Policy mandates 1 GW of demand response by 2025. States like Tamil Nadu pilot programs where 50 industrial units adjust loads via IoT-enabled systems.
learn.stat1: India’s demand response potential: 15 GW by 2030.
learn.stat2: Global demand response market to hit $32B by 2026.
learn.stat3: Participating industries save 10-15% on energy bills.
learn.stat4: Tamil Nadu’s pilot reduced peak demand by 8% in 2022.

learn.title: Bifacial Solar Panels
learn.intro: Bifacial panels generate power from both sides, boosting efficiency by up to 30%. They capture reflected light from surfaces like rooftops or water, making them ideal for India’s sunny climate.
learn.c1_text: Standard panels only use front-side sunlight. Bifacial panels add 10-30% output by absorbing reflected light. A 300W panel could yield 390W in ideal conditions, equivalent to adding 10% more panels.
learn.c2_text: These panels use transparent cells and glass-on-glass frames. They perform best with elevated mounting (e.g., 1m above ground) and reflective surfaces like white gravel or water bodies, increasing albedo effect.
learn.c3_text: India’s 50 GW solar target includes 20 GW bifacial projects. The 2023 National Solar Mission offers 10% higher tariffs for bifacial installations, with Andhra Pradesh leading at 1.2 GW deployed.
learn.stat1: India installed 6.5 GW bifacial solar in 2023.
learn.stat2: Bifacial panels increase LCOE by 5-10% but yield 20% higher energy.
learn.stat3: Andhra Pradesh’s bifacial farms save ₹2,000/crore annually.
learn.stat4: Global bifacial market to reach $100B by 2026.

learn.title: Solar Inverter Types
learn.intro: Inverters convert DC solar power to AC for homes. String, micro, and hybrid inverters offer trade-offs in cost, efficiency, and scalability, critical for India’s rooftop solar growth.
learn.c1_text: One inverter per panel array. Cost-effective but vulnerable—if one panel is shaded, output drops 20-30%. Ideal for small, unshaded rooftops.
learn.c2_text: One inverter per panel. Each operates independently, boosting system efficiency by 5-25%. Popular in India’s hilly regions where shading is common.
learn.c3_text: Combines solar DC/AC conversion with battery storage. Enables off-grid setups. India’s 2024 solar policy allows hybrid systems to qualify for 40% subsidy under PM-Surya.
learn.stat2: Micro inverters cost ₹10,000/kW vs ₹5,000/kW for string.
learn.stat3: Hybrid systems reduce grid dependency by 70%.
learn.stat4: PM-Surya targets 40 GW rooftop solar by 2030.

learn.title: Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs)
learn.intro: PPAs let renewable projects sell electricity long-term at fixed prices, reducing financing risks. India’s 2023 policy mandates PPAs for 80% of solar/wind projects, unlocking $100B+ investments.
learn.c1_text: A 25-year PPA locks in prices (e.g., ₹3.5/kWh). Developers avoid upfront costs, while buyers secure stable rates. Example: A Gujarat solar farm sells power to a retailer at fixed rates.
learn.c2_text: PPAs reduce capital costs by 40% by offloading financing. Developers use power purchase guarantees to secure loans at lower interest rates. Grid-connected projects bypass auctions.
learn.c3_text: India’s 2023 renewable policy requires PPAs for 80% of projects. Rajasthan’s Bhadla Solar Park, the world’s largest, uses PPAs to lock in ₹2.6/kWh for 25 years.
learn.stat2: Global PPA market to hit $300B by 2030.
learn.stat4: Bhadla Solar Park’s PPA price: ₹2.6/kWh (lowest globally).

learn.title: Hydrogen Color Codes
learn.intro: Grey (fossil), blue (captured CO2), and green (renewable) hydrogen differentiate production methods. Green hydrogen’s role in India’s net-zero plan hinges on 5 MT/year by 2030.
learn.c1_text: Electrolysis splits water using renewable electricity. 1 kg costs ₹180-₹250 (2023), down from ₹300 in 2020. India’s target: 5 MT/year green hydrogen by 2030.
learn.c2_text: Blue hydrogen uses natural gas + carbon capture (90% efficiency). Grey emits CO2 directly. India’s NTPC plans 1 MT/year blue hydrogen via coal gasification with CCS.
learn.c3_text: The National Hydrogen Mission targets 5 MT/year green hydrogen by 2030. Projects like Tata’s Gujarat plant use 100% renewable power, supported by ₹15,000 crore in subsidies.
learn.stat2: Green hydrogen cost to drop to ₹100/kg by 2030.
learn.stat3: NTPC’s blue hydrogen plant: 0.5 MT/year by 2025.
learn.stat4: Tata’s green plant: 20 kW electrolyzer operational in 2023.
